text: Last lesson made the case for writing a module once a pattern repeats two or three times. This lesson writes one in full: a real network module that takes a VNet name, an address space, and a subnet count as input, and hands back the IDs of the subnets it creates — the exact shape a compute or database module will need to plug into later.

By convention, a module folder splits into three files. variables.tf declares its interface: vnet_name and address_space as required strings and lists, subnet_count as an optional number defaulting to 2. Typing each variable means Terraform rejects a bad call — a number where a list was expected — at plan time, before anything touches a real resource.

main.tf holds the actual resources, reading each input back with var.vnet_name and var.address_space, the same var. syntax used in any root configuration. The subnet resource uses count to create several subnets at once, and cidrsubnet carves a non-overlapping slice of the address space for each one automatically — no hand-calculated CIDR ranges to keep in sync as subnet_count changes.

outputs.tf declares what the module hands back. subnet_ids uses the splat operator to collect the id of every subnet count created into one list. Calling the module from a root configuration looks like any other block: source points at the folder, and every other line matches one of the variables the module declared.

Outside the module, its outputs are reached with module dot the local name dot the output name — module.network.subnet_ids. That's the exact pattern the next lesson's composed environment relies on: one module's output becoming another module's input, chained together without ever copying a value by hand.

Three files, one folder, nothing exotic: typed inputs in, resources built from them in the middle, typed outputs back out. Next lesson pins this module to a specific version instead of always pulling whatever's newest, the same discipline already applied to provider versions back in Chapter 1.
